prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I moved my preferred configuration from my own opening first choice (IceCube, B039) to the optical lattice clock (B007), which I ranked second and which the committee supports far more broadly: three first places and six top-three rankings. As an instrument builder I judge it by the criteria I apply to any detector: a new measurement capability, controlled systematics and independent confirmation. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the light-shift problem by design, and Ye's group pushed strontium lattice clocks to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE have since reproduced and compared such clocks repeatedly. It already supports concrete science (millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constant variation, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy) and underpins the planned redefinition of the second. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, which matters for a Chair who wants a prize the committee can defend without a long argument over who is left out.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one several colleagues and I raised: this can be read as a continuation of the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion control) metrology prizes, and as an instrument achievement rather than a discovery. The SI second has not yet been redefined, so part of the impact is still prospective. Priority for early lattice-clock ideas (for example Lemonde's early strontium work, and the JILA collaborators) is also not fully captured by two names. A fair reading is that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured combs and single-ion control, whereas the neutral-atom lattice clock is a distinct invention and a distinct measurement regime. I do not think the overlap objection is disqualifying, but it is real.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B058) first, as a clean case of foundational quantum optics becoming an enabling platform, and flagged that Wallraff is missing from the credited names and that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may already cover the area.
responses.response: I take the point on Wallraff: the first strong-coupling experiment is a decisive experimental contribution, and a Blais, Schoelkopf and Girvin trio leaves the experimental credit incomplete, which weakens B058 as a three-name prize. Your own concern about the 2025 award also matters to me, because we should not return to superconducting circuits so soon. I cannot judge the physics of B058 in depth, so I am relying on you here, but on attribution alone B007 is stronger, and you ranked it second yourself.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked twisted bilayer graphene (B001) first and called it a rare surprise in a material with a direct theory-experiment loop, while placing the lattice clock fifth because of apparent overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
responses.response: I respect the B001 case and ranked it third myself, and I will not pretend to have the condensed-matter expertise to overrule you. Where I disagree is on the clock overlap. The 2005 prize covered combs and the 2012 prize covered single quantum systems such as trapped ions. The lattice clock with magic wavelengths, and the many-atom systematic control that comes with it, is a separate invention with confirmed 1e-18 performance across several labs. For B001, the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unresolved, and the credit question for Bistritzer and for Cao, as the lead experimental author, is real, so I see B001 as slightly less settled today. I would keep it as the leading alternative rather than dismissing it.

responses.point: Olsson ranked aberration-corrected electron optics (B030) first, as a genuine invention that transformed materials physics, and noted that the redefinition of the second is still prospective for the lattice clock.
responses.response: I agree with the principle that an experimental invention can deserve a Nobel Prize, and I favour that kind of work, so I take B030 seriously. The difference is breadth of support: you are the only member to rank it, and the STEM-corrector pioneers outside the credited names make a three-person split harder than you suggest. On the SI second, I accept that the redefinition is pending, but the performance and the intercomparisons are already established, and the clock does not need the redefinition to be a discovery-level measurement achievement.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the lattice clock first as an instrument-level discovery confirmed by nature and experiment, with a mature, two-person attribution, and he worried that the committee might see clocks as a technology milestone rather than a discovery.
responses.response: I agree with your assessment of maturity and attribution. On the technology-versus-discovery worry, I think the right answer is to word the citation around the invention and the new regime of measurement, not around a single application. Your comment that the ion-clock community may deserve joint recognition is the point I would like us to check: the 2012 prize addressed ion control, and I would want an expert reviewer to confirm that no ion-clock contribution is so closely tied to the lattice-clock result that two names would be unfair.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first, with Cirac and Zoller second, and pointed out that the atomic-structure side of the clock is well understood and that the claim to priority for the lattice idea is not fully resolved by the supplied names.
responses.response: Your atomic-physics expertise reassures me on the physics. On B015, I ranked it fourth and still see it as a serious theory prize, but I share your worry that theory-only recognition after the 2012 experimental prize, and Zoller's overlap with B008, may split support. The 2022 and 2025 quantum-information prizes also make me hesitant to return to that area soon. I would rather settle on B007 and keep B015 out of the first tier.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes rather than a continuation.
Whether priority for early lattice-clock concepts (for example early strontium work) or ion-clock contributions requires adding or changing names.
My own first choice, IceCube (B039), remains attractive but needs a fair split of credit between Halzen, Karle and Spiering within a very large collaboration; I do not see that resolved.
Condensed-matter candidates (B001, B023) are outside my expertise, and I would want expert reviewers to confirm the credit allocation before I rank them higher.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B007 or B001. For disclosure: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, and B039 (IceCube) is in my own broad field of astroparticle physics and neutrino astronomy, but nothing in my profile indicates a membership of or direct collaboration with IceCube or the credited individuals.
